name: G10 / Garolite (fiberglass-epoxy laminate)
summary: A solid fiberglass-reinforced epoxy laminate sheet — the same class of material as circuit-board substrate — used as a build surface rather than a coating. Its standout property is gripping nylon and TPU without any glue while still self-releasing on cooling. Aftermarket only; no major printer OEM ships it as a stock plate.
surface_makeup: Woven glass cloth impregnated with epoxy resin and cured under heat and pressure into a rigid composite laminate (typically ~0.5 mm when mounted on a magnetic flex plate). Non-conductive, low water absorption, low thermal expansion. It is a solid sheet, not a sprayed or powder-applied coating, so there is no coating layer to wear through.
manufacturers: generic AliExpress/Amazon G10 fiberglass sheet vendors

filament_compatibility.notes: Vendors state no release agent needed; releases on cooling without a spatula.
Specialty PLA blends behave as base PLA on this surface; the laminate's grip does not over-bond silk the way tacky low-temp surfaces can.
Abrasive CF-filled PLA is a good match here: the laminate is a solid composite with no thin coating for filled filaments to score through.
Generally no glue needed — G10 does not develop the aggressive chemical bond PETG forms with smooth PEI or bare glass.
Treated as PETG-equivalent; not separately documented by vendors (inferred from copolyester behavior).

filament_compatibility.adhesion_aid: none, thin PVA glue if first layers lift
filament_compatibility.notes: Unfilled PET runs hotter and stiffer than PETG; not specifically covered by G10 vendors — extrapolated from PETG guidance.
CF fill raises stiffness and corner-lift force; brim recommended. Not vendor-documented for G10.
Not covered in G10 sources; treated as PLA-adjacent. Keep IPA away from the plate while a PVB part is still on it — PVB dissolves in IPA.

filament_compatibility.adhesion_aid: none to brim; adhesion promoter on large flats
filament_compatibility.notes: Sources conflict: one vendor lists ABS/ASA at 100-120 C on its G10-family plate, another documents G10 only for PLA/PETG/nylon at 55-70 C and does not cover ABS at all. Enclosure matters more than the plate for warp.

filament_compatibility.adhesion_aid: none to brim; adhesion promoter on large flats
filament_compatibility.notes: Same conflicting-source caveat as ABS. Use a brim on large footprints.
Glass-filled ABS warps less but pulls harder at corners; not vendor-documented on G10.
Not covered in G10 sources; extrapolated from ABS/styrenic behavior.
Standout strength versus PEI: G10 grips TPU at room/ambient temperature and does not fuse to it, so no heat and no release agent are needed.
Firmer TPU grades release cleanly; the low-fusing behavior is the main reason flexible printers pick G10 over PEI.
Softer grades are the ones most likely to fuse into PEI; run the bed cool or unheated on G10 to keep release easy.
Softer TPE compounds are not separately documented on G10; start unheated and raise bed temp only if the first layer lifts.
Copolyester elastomer (TPEE class) behaves between PETG and TPU; not documented for G10.

filament_compatibility.adhesion_aid: none (optional thin PVA for a smoother bottom)
filament_compatibility.notes: The headline use case. Multiple community reports state garolite prints nylon with no glue at all, where PEI plates need Magigoo PA or a glue stick. A thin PVA layer is optional purely for surface finish, not adhesion.
PA6 grades adhere directly; dry the filament thoroughly — moisture, not the plate, is the usual first-layer failure with nylon.
Lower-moisture PA12 runs cooler and is one of the easiest nylons on this surface.
CF-filled nylon (PAHT-CF class) adheres without adhesive per Bambu community reports; no coating to abrade.
Same no-glue behavior as other CF nylons.

filament_compatibility.adhesion_aid: adhesion promoter (Magigoo PC or equivalent) recommended
filament_compatibility.notes: Bed temp taken from carbon/G10-family vendor guidance; unverified whether plain G10 without a CF blend performs identically. Enclosure strongly recommended.
Blend sits between ABS and PC in warp force; not separately documented on G10.

filament_compatibility.adhesion_aid: PP-specific adhesion promoter or packing tape required
filament_compatibility.notes: Not covered by any G10 source. PP sticks reliably only to itself or a dedicated promoter on essentially every surface — assume the same here.
Glass fill reduces warp somewhat but does not change the adhesion problem. Undocumented on G10.
Not covered in G10 sources. Keep the plate dry — PVA is water-soluble and residue left on a laminate surface will go tacky in humid air.
Undocumented for G10; treated as PVA-equivalent. Normally only contacts the plate as an interface/support layer.

Some vendors market a 'high-temp upgrade' G10 sheet alongside PEEK/PEKK/ULTEM name-drops, but no bed-temp or adhesion data was found and PEEK bed temps (130-160 C) exceed anything verified for this laminate. Do not assume compatibility.
Same as PEEK — marketing mentions exist, verified data does not.

preparation: First use needs nothing beyond a wash: soap and warm water or an IPA wipe to remove handling oils and shipping residue, then dry fully before mounting on the magnetic base. Vendors consistently state no glue is required for the materials G10 is bought for (PLA, PETG, TPU, nylon), so resist the urge to pre-coat it — an adhesive layer mostly negates the self-release behavior you paid for. Per-print prep is just a check that the surface is dry and free of stray plastic flecks; the texture hides light debris but a fragment under the first layer still shows. Note that a scuff-and-sand routine is often recommended for garolite in community lore, but no vendor documentation confirming a sanding grit or interval was found, so treat sanding as unverified rather than standard practice. On Bambu machines, disable automatic plate detection or select a compatible plate code (vendors suggest a High Temp/Smooth PEI profile as a workaround) — the printer cannot identify a third-party G10 sheet and will otherwise refuse or mis-profile the job.
cleaning: Routine cleaning is light-duty by design; vendors describe the textured laminate as low-maintenance and needing little cleanup between prints. Wipe cold with 90%+ IPA to lift finger oils, or wash with warm water and unscented dish soap for a deeper reset, then dry completely — this is a glass-epoxy composite and trapped moisture in the texture will show up as first-layer inconsistency. Remove stuck plastic flecks with a plastic scraper or a fingernail; avoid steel blades, which can gouge the resin-rich top layer between glass fibers. No G10-specific solvent guidance exists in the sources, so apply the same caution used for other composite surfaces: skip acetone and other aggressive solvents, which attack epoxy binders, and never soak the plate if it is bonded to a steel flex sheet — the mounting adhesive is the weak link, not the laminate.
model_removal: Cold release is the whole trick with this surface: vendors describe it as sticky when heated and letting go 'like magic' once cool, with parts self-releasing below roughly 70 C. Let the bed drop to room temperature and most prints either pop off on their own or come free with a light flex of the sheet if it is mounted on a magnetic spring-steel carrier. For a part that is still holding at ambient, run a bead of IPA around the print's corners and let it wick under the perimeter — it breaks the seal in seconds. A spatula is rarely needed; if you reach for one, use plastic and enter at a corner rather than prying from the middle. Do not try to remove parts hot — at bed temperature the laminate is at peak grip and you will either tear the part or lever against the plate.
stuck_print_recovery: No G10-specific recovery procedure is documented, so use the general escalation ladder and stop at the first thing that works. Start by simply waiting: let the plate reach full room temperature, because most 'stuck' prints on this surface are just prints removed too early. Next, flex the sheet progressively from one corner if it is on a magnetic flex plate, which is the fastest release for anything with a large footprint. If it still holds, wick IPA under the print edge and give it a minute to creep under the first layer. For big flat parts, work a length of dental floss or fishing line under one edge and saw side-to-side along the bond line. Only then reach for a thin plastic spatula, entering at a corner and never forcing from the center. Do not use a metal blade or a hammer-and-chisel approach — the glass-epoxy laminate will chip, and unlike a coating it cannot be touched up. A freezer cycle of 10-15 minutes is a reasonable last resort for a flex-mounted sheet, though it is undocumented for G10 specifically and risks condensation on a composite plate.
lifespan_notes: Durability is one of the reasons buyers choose this surface — comparison sources call out excellent longevity with high-temperature materials, and because the plate is a solid laminate rather than a coating there is nothing to wear through and expose a different substrate underneath. Wear shows as gradual polishing of the texture in the high-use center zone and, eventually, resin loss that exposes glass fibers; at that point adhesion drops and the sheet is replaced outright since recoating is not an option. On flex-mounted versions the adhesive bond to the steel carrier tends to fail before the laminate does, particularly if the plate is repeatedly soaked or run above its rated bed temperature. No vendor publishes a print-count or replacement interval, so treat 'replace when adhesion no longer returns after a soap wash' as the practical rule.

price.notes: ~250 mm class. Darkmoon3D G10 plate listed at $38.99 (184/256/320/350 mm sizes); generic Amazon/AliExpress fiberglass sheets commonly $20-30 for 220-257 mm. Bare sheets are cheaper than magnet-mounted flex plate versions.

additional_notes: Notably lighter than glass or steel alternatives, and commonly sold pre-mounted to a magnetic flex plate for quick-swap use on Bambu, Creality and Ender-style beds. The material is the same class used for printed circuit boards, so bare sheets are also widely available from industrial plastics suppliers and can be cut to size — a common DIY route. Bambu printers' automatic plate detection cannot identify third-party G10, so the feature has to be disabled or spoofed with another plate code. The single biggest reason to own one is nylon: multiple independent community reports describe printing any nylon with no adhesive at all, which is the one job PEI cannot do without Magigoo PA or a glue stick.

provenance.conflicts: ABS/ASA bed temperature: one vendor lists 100-120 C for its G10-family plate while another documents G10 only for PLA/PETG/nylon at 55-70 C and does not address ABS/ASA at all; it is unclear whether the 100-120 C figure came from a carbon-blended sibling product rather than plain G10. The same ambiguity applies to the PC 110-120 C figure. No source gives a hard maximum surface temperature for the laminate — the 130 C value recorded here is the generic continuous rating for glass-epoxy laminate, not a vendor-published plate spec. Vendor 'high-temp upgrade' G10 sheets name-drop PEEK/PEKK/ULTEM with no supporting data; recorded as avoid pending evidence. Prep (scuffing/sanding), cleaning solvents, and stuck-print recovery are not documented for G10 anywhere in the sources and the guidance here is extrapolated from comparable composite surfaces. PP, PVA and BVOH compatibility is entirely inferred.
